notes:
1. Science and Technology in Agriculture — Meaning and Purpose

  • Science and technology have transformed agriculture from a mainly traditional activity into an increasingly knowledge-based and technology-driven sector.
  • Modern agricultural technology seeks to increase productivity, improve farmer income, reduce production risks and use land, water, labour, fertilisers and energy more efficiently.
  • Agricultural science also increasingly focuses on resource conservation and climate resilience.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agricultural Technology → Productivity + Income + Efficiency + Risk Reduction + Sustainability

2. Major Areas of Agricultural Technology

Important applications include:

  • Improved seeds.
  • Irrigation technology.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Soil testing.
  • Pest management.
  • Biotechnology.
  • Weather forecasting.
  • Digital advisory systems.
  • Remote sensing.
  • GIS and GPS.
  • Drones.
  • Artificial intelligence.
  • IoT.
  • Post-harvest technology.

3. Agricultural Research — Role

Agricultural research develops:

  • Improved crop varieties.
  • Better cultivation methods.
  • Pest and disease-control techniques.
  • Efficient irrigation systems.
  • Farm machinery.
  • Livestock and allied-sector technologies.

Research is carried out through:

  • Agricultural universities.
  • Specialised research institutions.
  • Government agencies.
  • Scientific organisations.

4. ICAR — Apex Agricultural Research Organisation

  • ICAR stands for Indian Council of Agricultural Research.
  • It is the apex national organisation coordinating agricultural research, education and related scientific activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

ICAR → Indian Council of Agricultural Research

ICAR → Apex Agricultural Research Organisation

5. Agricultural Universities and Extension

  • Agricultural universities contribute to research, teaching and extension.
  • Agricultural extension connects scientific institutions with farmers.

Extension can provide guidance on:

  • Crop selection.
  • Improved varieties.
  • Irrigation.
  • Fertiliser use.
  • Pest management.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Weather.
  • Market information.
📌 Must-Memorise

Extension → Science Reaches Farmer

6. Research-to-Farm Chain

Research

→ Extension

→ Farmer Adoption

→ Higher Productivity

📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core knowledge-transfer chain.

7. Seed Quality — Productivity Role

  • Seed quality is one of the most important determinants of crop productivity.
  • Scientific plant breeding can develop varieties with higher yields, shorter duration and greater resistance to pests, diseases and environmental stress.

8. HYV — High-Yielding Variety

  • HYV stands for High-Yielding Variety.
  • HYVs played an important role in the Green Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

HYV → High-Yielding Variety

9. Improved Crop Varieties — Major Traits

Scientific breeding can develop varieties with:

  • Higher yield.
  • Shorter duration.
  • Disease resistance.
  • Pest resistance.
  • Drought tolerance.
  • Flood tolerance.
  • Salinity tolerance.
  • Improved nutritional quality.

10. Hybrid Seeds

  • Hybrid seeds are produced by crossing genetically different parental lines.
  • Hybridisation seeks to combine desirable traits.
  • Hybrid crops may exhibit hybrid vigour.
  • Saved hybrid seed may not reproduce the same performance in the next generation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hybrid Seed → Cross of Different Parental Lines

11. HYV vs Hybrid Seed

  • HYV and hybrid seed are not identical concepts.
  • An improved high-yielding variety need not necessarily be a commercial hybrid.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

HYV ≠ Hybrid Seed

12. Seed Replacement and Seed Technology

  • Seed replacement means replacing poor-quality or degenerated seed with certified or quality seed.
  • The seed-technology chain broadly includes:

Breeding

→ Multiplication

→ Certification

→ Storage

→ Distribution

13. Agricultural Biotechnology — Meaning

  • Agricultural biotechnology uses biological processes and organisms to improve agricultural production.

Major techniques include:

  • Plant breeding.
  • Tissue culture.
  • Molecular methods.
  • Marker-assisted selection.
  • Genetic engineering.
  • Genome editing.

14. Genetically Modified Crops

  • A crop developed through insertion or modification of specific genetic material may be described as a genetically modified crop.

15. Bt Cotton

  • Bt cotton is a genetically modified cotton crop developed for resistance against specified insect pests.
  • Bt refers to Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt cotton contains genes derived from this bacterium.
  • It is particularly associated with resistance to certain bollworms.
  • Bt cotton was commercially introduced in India in 2002.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bt → Bacillus thuringiensis

Bt Cotton in India → 2002

16. Bt Cotton — Important Limitation

  • Bt cotton was developed for resistance to specified insect pests.
  • It does not provide universal resistance against every pest or disease.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bt Cotton ≠ Resistance to Every Pest

17. Marker-Assisted Selection

  • Marker-Assisted Selection uses identifiable DNA markers linked to desirable traits.
  • It can make conventional breeding faster and more precise.
  • It does not necessarily involve inserting foreign genes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Marker-Assisted Selection → DNA Markers

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Marker-Assisted Selection ≠ Necessarily Genetic Engineering

18. Genome Editing

  • Genome editing modifies specific parts of an organism's DNA.
  • Potential agricultural uses include:
  • Pest resistance.
  • Disease resistance.
  • Stress tolerance.
  • Quality improvement.
  • Climate resilience.

19. Biotechnology — Major Concerns

Agricultural biotechnology requires attention to:

  • Biosafety.
  • Environmental effects.
  • Regulation.
  • Farmer access.
  • Affordability.

20. Soil Testing — Meaning and Purpose

  • Soil testing scientifically examines the physical and chemical condition of soil.
  • Its main purpose is to match fertiliser application with actual field and crop requirements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Soil Testing → Scientific Assessment of Soil Condition

21. Soil Testing — Major Parameters

Soil testing can assess:

  • pH.
  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
  • Micronutrients.
  • Organic carbon.
  • Salinity.

22. NPK

  • NPK refers to:
  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
📌 Must-Memorise

N → Nitrogen

P → Phosphorus

K → Potassium

23. Site-Specific Nutrient Management

  • Site-specific nutrient management adjusts fertiliser application according to the actual condition of a particular field.
  • It can improve nutrient-use efficiency and reduce unnecessary fertiliser use.

24. Biofertilisers

  • Biofertilisers contain beneficial microorganisms that improve nutrient availability.
  • Some improve nitrogen availability.
  • Others help mobilise phosphorus.

25. Rhizobium

  • Rhizobium bacteria are especially important in association with leguminous crops.
  • They support biological nitrogen fixation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rhizobium → Legumes → Nitrogen Fixation

26. Integrated Nutrient Management

  • Integrated Nutrient Management combines chemical and biological nutrient sources.

It may include:

  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Organic manures.
  • Biofertilisers.
  • Crop residues.
  • Its aim is to sustain productivity while protecting long-term soil fertility.

27. Modern Irrigation Technology

  • Modern irrigation aims to provide the required amount of water at the correct time while reducing wastage.
  • Major technologies include drip irrigation, sprinkler irrigation, fertigation, sensors and automation.

28. Drip Irrigation

  • Drip irrigation delivers water directly near the root zone through pipes and emitters.
  • It can reduce evaporation and runoff.
  • It is particularly useful for several horticultural crops and water-scarce areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Drip → Root-Zone Application

29. Sprinkler Irrigation

  • Sprinkler irrigation distributes water through pressurised nozzles.
  • Water is applied in a pattern similar to rainfall.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sprinkler → Pressurised Spray

30. Drip vs Sprinkler

  • Drip → Water near roots.
  • Sprinkler → Water sprayed across field.

31. Fertigation

  • Fertigation means application of fertilisers through irrigation water.
  • It allows more precise nutrient application.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fertigation → Fertiliser + Irrigation

32. Soil-Moisture Sensors and Automated Irrigation

  • Soil-moisture sensors can indicate when crops require water.
  • Automated irrigation systems can switch irrigation on or off based on sensor readings or programmed conditions.
  • These technologies reduce unnecessary water use.

33. Farm Mechanisation — Meaning

  • Farm mechanisation uses machines and equipment to perform agricultural operations.
  • It improves timeliness and operational efficiency.

34. Major Farm Machines

Important machinery includes:

  • Tractors.
  • Power tillers.
  • Seed drills.
  • Mechanical transplanters.
  • Sprayers.
  • Harvesters.
  • Threshers.
  • Combine harvesters.

35. Seed Drill

  • A seed drill places seed at controlled depth and spacing.
  • It can improve germination and reduce unnecessary seed use.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seed Drill → Controlled Depth + Spacing

36. Mechanical Transplanters

  • Mechanical transplanters reduce labour requirements in crops such as paddy.

37. Combine Harvester

  • A combine harvester performs cutting, threshing and grain separation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Combine Harvester → Cut + Thresh + Separate Grain

38. Laser Land Levelling

  • Laser land levelling uses laser-guided equipment to create a more uniform field surface.
  • A uniform surface improves irrigation efficiency and reduces uneven water distribution.

39. Custom Hiring

  • Custom-hiring centres allow farmers to rent machinery instead of purchasing it.
  • They are especially useful for small and marginal farmers who cannot economically own expensive machines.
📌 Must-Memorise

Custom Hiring → Machinery on Rent

40. Precision Agriculture — Meaning

  • Precision agriculture applies farm inputs according to the specific requirements of different parts of a field.
  • It recognises that soil fertility, moisture, pests and crop conditions vary within the same field.
📌 Must-Memorise

Precision Agriculture → Location-Specific Input Management

41. Precision Agriculture — Major Technologies

Precision farming can use:

  • GPS.
  • Sensors.
  • Satellite imagery.
  • Drones.
  • Soil maps.
  • Digital farm records.

42. Variable Rate Technology — VRT

  • VRT stands for Variable Rate Technology.
  • It applies different quantities of inputs to different areas of a field.

It can vary:

  • Seed.
  • Fertiliser.
  • Pesticide.
  • Irrigation.
📌 Must-Memorise

VRT → Variable Input Rate by Location

43. Precision Agriculture — Benefits

Potential benefits include:

  • Lower unnecessary input expenditure.
  • Reduced fertiliser and pesticide overuse.
  • Earlier crop-stress detection.
  • Better yields.
  • Lower environmental damage.

44. Remote Sensing

  • Remote sensing collects information about the Earth's surface without direct physical contact.

Agricultural uses include:

  • Crop-area estimation.
  • Crop-health monitoring.
  • Drought assessment.
  • Flood assessment.
  • Soil-moisture analysis.
  • Vegetation monitoring.
  • Yield estimation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Remote Sensing → Information Without Direct Contact

45. GIS — Geographic Information System

  • GIS stores, analyses and displays geographically referenced information.

Agricultural uses include mapping:

  • Soil.
  • Rainfall.
  • Irrigation.
  • Land use.
  • Groundwater.
📌 Must-Memorise

GIS → Geographic Information System

46. GPS — Global Positioning System

GPS can assist with:

  • Machinery guidance.
  • Field-boundary mapping.
  • Recording soil-sampling locations.
📌 Must-Memorise

GPS → Location and Positioning

47. Remote Sensing vs GIS vs GPS

  • Remote sensing → Collects information.
  • GIS → Analyses spatial information.
  • GPS → Provides location.
📌 Must-Memorise

Observe → Analyse → Locate

48. Agricultural Drones

  • Agricultural drones are unmanned aerial vehicles carrying cameras, sensors or spraying systems.

They can be used for:

  • Crop monitoring.
  • Field mapping.
  • Pest detection.
  • Disease detection.
  • Crop assessment.
  • Field inspection.
  • Targeted spraying under applicable rules.

49. Multispectral Imaging

  • Multispectral cameras capture information beyond normal visible light.
  • They can identify crop stress before it becomes easily visible to the human eye.

50. Drone Spraying — Benefits and Risks

Potential benefit:

  • Reduced direct human exposure during difficult spraying operations.

Risks include:

  • Chemical drift.
  • Uneven application.
  • Improper operation.
  • Agricultural drone use therefore requires trained operators and appropriate regulation.

51. Artificial Intelligence — AI

  • AI stands for Artificial Intelligence.
  • AI can analyse large volumes of agricultural data to identify useful patterns.

52. AI — Agricultural Applications

AI can assist in:

  • Pest identification.
  • Disease detection.
  • Yield prediction.
  • Weather-based advice.
  • Irrigation scheduling.
  • Market and price analysis.

53. IoT — Internet of Things

  • IoT refers to networks of connected sensors and devices that collect and exchange data.
📌 Must-Memorise

IoT → Internet of Things

54. IoT — Agricultural Uses

Connected sensors can monitor:

  • Soil moisture.
  • Temperature.
  • Humidity.
  • Water levels.
  • Livestock movement.
  • Greenhouse conditions.

55. Smart Farming — Feedback Loop

Sensor Collects Data

→ Software Analyses Data

→ Farmer Receives Advice

→ Farm Operation Adjusted

📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core smart-farming loop.

56. AI — Data Quality Limitation

  • AI recommendations depend on the quality of the data and models used.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Poor Data → Poor AI Recommendation

57. Digital Agriculture — Meaning

  • Digital agriculture uses information and communication technologies to support farm decisions.

Major tools include:

  • Mobile applications.
  • SMS services.
  • Websites.
  • Digital marketplaces.
  • Call centres.
  • Online advisories.

58. Digital Advisory Services

Digital systems can provide:

  • Weather information.
  • Crop recommendations.
  • Market prices.
  • Pest alerts.
  • Government-scheme information.
  • Agricultural-input information.

59. Digital Agriculture — Adoption Requirements

Effective digital adoption requires:

  • Reliable connectivity.
  • Affordable technology.
  • Farmer training.
  • Local-language interfaces.

60. Digital Markets

  • Digital platforms can widen farmer access to buyers and prices.
  • However, online markets still depend on physical transport, grading, storage and logistics.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Digital Market ≠ Replacement for Physical Infrastructure

61. Digital Payments in Agriculture

  • Digital payments can improve transparency in transactions involving farmers, traders, banks and government agencies.

62. Agro-Meteorology

  • Agro-meteorology studies the relationship between weather and agriculture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agro-Meteorology → Weather + Agriculture

63. Important Weather Factors for Agriculture

Important variables include:

  • Rainfall.
  • Temperature.
  • Humidity.
  • Wind.
  • Sunlight.

These affect:

  • Crop growth.
  • Water availability.
  • Disease conditions.
  • Evaporation.
  • Photosynthesis.

64. Weather Forecasting — Farm Decisions

Forecasts can guide:

  • Sowing.
  • Irrigation.
  • Fertiliser application.
  • Pesticide spraying.
  • Harvesting.

65. Short-Term and Seasonal Forecasts

  • Short-term forecasts help farmers respond to immediate weather conditions.
  • Seasonal forecasts assist longer-term crop planning.

66. Early-Warning Systems

Early warnings can help farmers prepare for:

  • Cyclones.
  • Floods.
  • Droughts.
  • Heat waves.
  • Heavy rainfall.

67. Integrated Pest Management — IPM

  • IPM stands for Integrated Pest Management.
  • It combines several pest-management techniques while reducing excessive dependence on chemicals.
📌 Must-Memorise

IPM → Integrated Pest Management

68. IPM — Major Components

IPM can combine:

  • Biological control.
  • Cultural practices.
  • Mechanical control.
  • Resistant varieties.
  • Need-based chemical pesticides.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

IPM ≠ Complete Ban on Pesticides

69. Biological Control

  • Biological control uses natural predators, parasites or microorganisms to control agricultural pests.

70. Pheromone Traps

  • Pheromone traps use chemical signals to attract specific insect pests.
  • They can be used for pest monitoring and targeted control.

71. Crop Diagnostics and Pest Surveillance

Modern pest and disease surveillance can use:

  • Laboratory testing.
  • Digital imaging.
  • Remote sensing.
  • Sensors.
  • Mobile applications.
  • Drones.
  • Early detection can reduce crop losses.

72. Post-Harvest Technology — Meaning

  • Post-harvest technology protects agricultural produce after harvest.

It includes:

  • Cleaning.
  • Drying.
  • Grading.
  • Packaging.
  • Storage.
  • Processing.
  • Transportation.

73. Scientific Warehousing

  • Scientific warehousing protects grain against moisture, pests, rodents and contamination.
  • Proper drying before storage is particularly important.

74. Cold Storage

  • Cold storage keeps agricultural products at controlled low temperatures.

It is especially important for:

  • Fruits and vegetables.
  • Milk.
  • Meat.
  • Fish.

75. Cold Chain

  • A cold chain maintains controlled temperature continuously from production to final market.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pre-Cooling

→ Cold Storage

→ Refrigerated Transport

→ Distribution

76. Cold Storage vs Cold Chain

  • Cold storage → A single temperature-controlled facility.
  • Cold chain → Continuous temperature-controlled system across stages.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cold Storage ≠ Cold Chain

77. Food Processing

  • Food processing can add value to agricultural produce.
  • It can also reduce post-harvest losses and improve farmer income.

Examples include:

  • Milk → Dairy products.
  • Tomato → Processed products.
  • Fruits → Juice / pulp.
  • Grain → Flour and other products.
  • Sugarcane → Sugar / ethanol.

78. Tissue Culture

  • Tissue culture grows small pieces of plant tissue under sterile laboratory conditions.
  • It can rapidly produce large numbers of genetically similar plants.
  • It can also produce disease-free planting material under suitable conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tissue Culture → Sterile Laboratory Plant Multiplication

79. Tissue Culture — Major Uses

Tissue culture is important in:

  • Commercial horticulture.
  • Banana cultivation.
  • Ornamental plants.
  • Rapid multiplication of desirable planting material.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tissue Culture ≠ Genetic Modification

80. Protected Cultivation

  • Protected cultivation grows crops in structures where environmental conditions are partly controlled.

Examples include:

  • Greenhouses.
  • Polyhouses.
  • Shade-net structures.

81. Protected Cultivation — Benefits

It can help manage:

  • Temperature.
  • Humidity.
  • Light.
  • Pest exposure.

It is especially useful for:

  • High-value vegetables.
  • Flowers.
  • Nursery plants.

82. Hydroponics

  • Hydroponics grows plants without conventional soil using a water-based nutrient solution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hydroponics → Nutrient Solution, No Conventional Soil

83. Aeroponics

  • Aeroponics grows plants with roots suspended in air and supplied with nutrient mist.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aeroponics → Roots in Air + Nutrient Mist

84. Hydroponics vs Aeroponics

  • Hydroponics → Roots receive nutrient solution.
  • Aeroponics → Suspended roots receive nutrient mist.

85. Tamil Nadu — Need for Agricultural Technology

  • Tamil Nadu's diverse agro-climatic conditions and water constraints make scientific agricultural technology especially important.

86. TNAU — Tamil Nadu Agricultural University

  • TNAU stands for Tamil Nadu Agricultural University.
  • It is located in Coimbatore.
  • It contributes to agricultural education, research and extension.
📌 Must-Memorise

TNAU → Tamil Nadu Agricultural University → Coimbatore

87. TNAU — Major Areas of Contribution

TNAU contributes to:

  • Crop improvement.
  • Agricultural engineering.
  • Soil science.
  • Horticulture.
  • Extension.
  • Agricultural research.

88. Tamil Nadu — Micro-Irrigation

  • Drip and sprinkler irrigation are especially important because many parts of Tamil Nadu face water scarcity.
  • Micro-irrigation can improve water-use efficiency in:
  • Sugarcane.
  • Banana.
  • Coconut.
  • Vegetables.
  • Horticultural crops.

89. Tamil Nadu — Precision Farming and Mechanisation

  • Precision farming can combine irrigation, fertigation, improved planting material and scientific crop management.
  • Mechanisation is increasingly used for land preparation, transplanting, harvesting and post-harvest activities.
  • Paddy transplanters and harvesters can reduce labour constraints.

90. Tamil Nadu — Dual Monsoon and Weather Advisories

  • Tamil Nadu receives rainfall from both the southwest and northeast monsoons.
  • Weather-based advisories are therefore important for:
  • Sowing.
  • Irrigation.
  • Pest management.
  • Harvesting.

91. Tamil Nadu — Fisheries and Coastal Technology

  • Tamil Nadu's long coastline makes marine and fisheries technology important.
  • Marine forecasting supports safer and more efficient fishing.
  • Scientific aquaculture methods can improve productivity and management.

104. TNPSC Traps

  • ICAR is the apex national agricultural research organisation.
  • Agricultural extension connects research institutions with farmers.
  • HYV and hybrid seed are not identical.
  • Hybridisation does not necessarily mean genetic engineering.
  • All improved crops are not GM crops.
  • Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt cotton is a genetically modified cotton crop.
  • Bt cotton was commercially introduced in India in 2002.
  • Bt cotton resists specified pests, not every pest.
  • Marker-assisted selection does not necessarily insert foreign genes.
  • Genome editing and hybridisation are different.
  • Soil testing assesses much more than soil colour.
  • NPK means nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Rhizobium is linked with nitrogen fixation in legumes.
  • Biofertilisers contain beneficial microorganisms.
  • Drip and sprinkler irrigation are different.
  • Fertigation means fertiliser through irrigation.
  • Mechanisation is broader than tractor use.
  • Seed drills control depth and spacing.
  • Combine harvesters cut, thresh and separate grain.
  • Custom hiring means machinery rental.
  • Precision agriculture means location-specific management.
  • VRT changes input quantities according to field conditions.
  • Remote sensing, GIS and GPS perform different functions.
  • A drone is a platform; remote sensing is an information-gathering method.
  • Multispectral imaging can detect crop stress.
  • AI depends on good-quality data.
  • IoT means Internet of Things.
  • Digital markets still require physical transport and storage.
  • Agro-meteorology links weather and agriculture.
  • IPM does not mean zero pesticide use.
  • Cold storage and cold chain are different.
  • Tissue culture is not genetic modification.
  • Hydroponics and aeroponics are different.
  • TNAU is in Coimbatore.
  • Tamil Nadu's water constraints make micro-irrigation important.
  • Tamil Nadu receives both southwest and northeast monsoon rainfall.
  • Weather advisories are important for Tamil Nadu farming.
  • Tamil Nadu's coastline makes marine and fisheries technology important.
  • Technology must be affordable, accessible and supported by farmer training.
  • Technology alone cannot improve agriculture without adoption and infrastructure.

  • VRT function? → Applies different input quantities to different parts of a field.
  • Remote sensing? → Collects information without direct contact.
  • GIS full form? → Geographic Information System.
  • GPS function? → Location and positioning.
  • Remote sensing vs GIS vs GPS? → Collects, analyses, locates.
  • Agricultural drone uses? → Monitoring, mapping, pest detection and regulated spraying.
  • Multispectral imaging? → Detects crop stress.
  • AI uses? → Pest detection, yield forecasting, weather advice, irrigation and market analysis.
  • IoT full form? → Internet of Things.
  • IoT can monitor? → Soil moisture, temperature, humidity, water levels and livestock.
  • Smart-farming loop? → Sensor → Data → Analysis → Advice → Action.
  • Digital agriculture uses? → Apps, SMS, websites, digital markets and advisories.
  • Agro-meteorology? → Weather + Agriculture.
  • Weather forecasts help with? → Sowing, irrigation, fertilisation, spraying and harvest.
  • IPM full form? → Integrated Pest Management.
  • IPM components? → Biological, cultural, mechanical, resistant varieties and need-based chemicals.
  • Does IPM ban all pesticides? → No.
  • Pheromone trap use? → Monitoring/control of specific insect pests.
  • Post-harvest technology includes? → Cleaning, drying, grading, storage, processing and transport.
  • Cold storage? → One low-temperature facility.
  • Cold chain? → Continuous temperature-controlled chain.
  • Tissue culture? → Sterile laboratory multiplication of plant tissue.
  • Tissue culture and GM same? → No.
  • Important tissue-culture crop? → Banana.
  • Protected cultivation examples? → Greenhouse, polyhouse and shade net.
  • Hydroponics? → Nutrient solution without conventional soil.
  • Aeroponics? → Roots in air supplied with nutrient mist.
  • TNAU full form? → Tamil Nadu Agricultural University.
  • TNAU location? → Coimbatore.
  • Why micro-irrigation important in Tamil Nadu? → Water scarcity.
  • Important Tamil Nadu technologies? → Drip, fertigation, precision farming, mechanisation and weather advisories.
  • Why weather advisory especially useful in Tamil Nadu? → Dependence on both southwest and northeast monsoons.
  • Why fisheries technology important in Tamil Nadu? → Long coastline and significant fisheries activity.
  • Core technology chain? → Research → Improved Inputs → Precision Cultivation → Monitoring → Harvest → Storage → Processing → Market.
